title: Blog Eight Device Security Best Practices for Today’s Workforce
summary: Explore eight device security best practices to protect endpoints, strengthen access, support Zero Trust, and secure today’s hybrid workforce.
body_markdown:
## **Key takeaways**


- Strong device security starts with trusted hardware, consistent configuration, and automated updates.
- Identity controls, endpoint security, and Zero Trust security help limit unauthorized access and lateral movement.
- Continuous device compliance and a frictionless user experience help organizations maintain protection across a hybrid workforce.


### Device security has become one of the most important parts of an organization’s overall defense strategy. Every endpoint represents a doorway into your environment, and attackers know it.


When a single device is compromised, it can quickly turn into credential theft, lateral movement, or data loss. The good news is that modern platforms, especially Windows 11 coupled with modern devices, provide a powerful security foundation. What matters most? How consistently they are deployed.


## Start with hardware-rooted security.


Strong security begins before the operating system even loads. When the hardware can verify its own integrity, everything built on top of it becomes more trustworthy.


Windows 11 sets a clear baseline here:


- It requires TPM 2.0, which gives us secure key storage and cryptographic operations.
- Secure Boot ensures the device starts with trusted firmware.
- Virtualization based security isolates sensitive processes so that even if something goes wrong in the OS, critical secrets remain protected.


The principle is simple. Choose devices that support modern security capabilities and make sure those capabilities are turned on. When the hardware is trustworthy, the rest of your security strategy becomes far more effective.


## Strengthen identity and access controls.


Identity is the new perimeter. If an attacker gets a user’s credentials, they can often bypass traditional defenses. That’s why strong authentication is essential.


Passwordless sign-in is one of the most effective improvements you can make. Windows Hello and FIDO2 keys have been around for a while, but passkeys take this a step further. A passkey replaces the password entirely with a cryptographic credential stored securely on the device. It can’t be phished, guessed, reused, or stolen in a database breach. When a user signs in with a passkey, they authenticate with something they have and something they are. It feels simple to the user, but it dramatically reduces risk.


Multifactor authentication should still be required everywhere. Conditional access adds another layer by evaluating device health, user risk, and location before granting access. This is the heart of Microsoft’s Zero Trust approach. Never assume trust. Always verify. It’s a mindset as much as a technology stack — and it dramatically reduces the chances of unauthorized access.


## Keep devices continuously updated.


Unpatched vulnerabilities remain one of the most common attack vectors. The fix is straightforward. Updates must be automatic, predictable, and enforced.


Windows Update for Business gives us a reliable way to orchestrate updates across the fleet. You can set deadlines, monitor compliance, and ensure devices receive security patches quickly. Drivers and firmware should also come from trusted sources. Application updates matter too, especially for browsers and productivity tools.


The goal is consistency. When every device is current, you eliminate a huge portion of preventable risk.


## Apply strong configuration baselines.


A secure device is a well configured device. Baselines help every endpoint meet your minimum standards and stay aligned over time.


Start with removing local admin rights for standard users. This one change blocks a wide range of attacks. Add application control to prevent unauthorized software from running. Use full disk encryption, such as BitLocker, to protect data at rest. Harden browsers with anti-phishing protections and isolation features. Enforce network controls like firewalls and secure DNS.


Microsoft’s security baselines for Windows 11 are a helpful reference, but you should tailor them to your environment. Again, the important part is consistency. When every device follows the same rules, your security posture becomes much easier to manage.


## Use modern endpoint protection and detection.


Traditional antivirus is no longer enough. Modern threats require behavioral analysis, cloud intelligence, and real-time response.


Microsoft Defender for Endpoint exemplifies modern protection — combining next-generation antivirus, endpoint detection and response, automated attack disruption, and rich telemetry. It also integrates with Microsoft’s threat intelligence, which helps identify emerging risks quickly.


Whichever solution you choose, make sure it provides visibility, speed, and the ability to respond to threats before they spread.


## Adopt Zero Trust network access.


Devices should not automatically trust internal networks. Zero Trust network access ensures that every connection is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted.


This approach reduces lateral movement and limits the blast radius of a compromised device. It also aligns well with hybrid work, where users connect from many locations. Conditional access, encrypted sessions, and continuous validation all play a role.


When the network treats every session as untrusted until proven otherwise, attackers have a much harder time moving around.


## Monitor device health and compliance continuously.


Security is not a one-time configuration. It is a state that must be maintained. Continuous monitoring keeps devices compliant and healthy.


Modern management platforms, such as Microsoft Intune, provide real time compliance reporting and automated remediation. You can track device inventory, evaluate risk, and integrate with SIEM and SOAR systems for deeper analysis.


Visibility is essential. When you know the state of your devices, you can act quickly when something drifts out of compliance.


## Prioritize user experience as a security control.


This part is often overlooked. When devices are slow, outdated, or frustrating to use, people find workarounds. Those workarounds usually weaken security.


A secure device should also be fast, stable, and simple to authenticate. Windows 11 helps here with passkeys, passwordless sign-in, automated updates, and built-in protections that do not require constant user interaction. When security feels natural, users stay within the guardrails.


Good user experience is not separate from security. It’s part of it.
